meaning: Originally a chief of the evil spirits of darkness, bearing the name Vaiśravaṇa; in later mythology the god of riches and treasure, regent of the northern quarter.

phonemes.desc: Short u as in “put”; k sharp and unaspirated.
The e is long āy-like “ay” in careful speech: Ku-BAAIR-uh. The name is of uncertain root.
Classical Sanskrit stresses the second syllable: ku-BE-ra; the final vowel is short.

pronunciation.note: He began as chief of the evil spirits of darkness and ended as the Hindu god of riches.

domains.title: God of Riches, the Northern Quarter
domains.subtitle: Lord of the Yakṣas, Guardian of the World’s Treasure
domains.lead: Kubera is the Hindu god of wealth and its lordly guardian: king of the yakṣas, the treasure-keeping spirits of the earth, regent of the north, and keeper of the nine treasures. From a Vedic chief of demons he rose — through Śiva’s favour and epic patronage — to the dignified treasurer of the gods, fat, jewelled, and mounted on his great white guardian-lion or his human-mule.

cards.name: Lord of the North
cards.desc: One of the four lokapālas, regents of the directions; his quarter is the north, seat of wealth.

cards.name: King of the Yakṣas
cards.desc: The treasure-spirits of earth serve him; his capital, Alakā, gleams on Mount Kailāsa’s flank.

cards.name: The Nine Treasures
cards.desc: Nidhi, the nine jewels of kingship, lie in his keeping — each a named power of abundance.

cards.name: The Money-Pot
cards.desc: His mongoose ejects jewels from its mouth in Buddhist form; his belly is the vault he guards.

mythology.lead: Kubera’s mythology is a success story: the demon-chief who became a god. The Veda knows him only as Vaiśravaṇa, the powerful one of the dark; the epics made him the friend of Rāma’s line, the builder of Laṅkā before Rāvaṇa took it, and the guardian whose aerial chariot Pushpaka still serves the righteous.

myths.title: The Lord of Laṅkā Before Rāvaṇa
myths.text: Kubera built the golden city of Laṅkā on the world’s far shore, served by the yakṣas and filled with his hoard. His half-brother Rāvaṇa, through austerities and violence, took the city and the flying chariot Pushpaka from him; Kubera withdrew north to mount Gandhamādana, and Laṅkā passed to the demons — the great city’s golden age remembered as his.

myths.title: The Aerial Car Pushpaka
myths.text: The epic’s greatest vehicle belonged to Kubera: the self-moving palace-car Pushpaka, won back from Rāvaṇa by Rāma and returned in the epic’s closing book to its maker’s friend. To ride Pushpaka is to command the wealth of the world from above — and Rāma, refusing it, set the moral: treasure serves, the righteous decline it.

myths.title: The Demon Who Won a God’s Favour
myths.text: The Purāṇas tell how Kubera, in an earlier cosmic round, performed austerities until Śiva granted him guardianship of the north and lordship of wealth. Some tellings begin him darker: a gluttonous yakṣa king whose eye was burnt by Paraśurāma’s glance — the scar that marks his images’ asymmetric face.

myths.title: Jambhala, the Buddha’s Treasurer
myths.text: Buddhism adopted him outright as Jambhala — black or golden, eared with the mongoose that spits gems, seated on a citron fruit. In this form he became the wealth-god of Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhism, his mantras recited in monasteries that formally renounce what he provides.

lore.syncretism: Kubera is Vaiśravaṇa in Buddhist lands, Jambhala in Tibet, and the model of every treasurer-god from the yakṣa-cults to the Japanese Bishamonten — the same northern regent under three names. The Greeks heard Plutus in him; the comparatists hear the Celtic Dagda’s cauldron in his inexhaustible pot.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every Indian shopkeeper’s ‘Kubera’s pot’ and every temple’s treasure-vault under his image keep his cult domestic and current. His name entered the vocabulary of plenty across Southeast Asia — the Khmer temples guard their riches under his northern gaze — and Jambhala thangkas remain among Tibetan art’s most beloved subjects.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kubera: the name of the world’s oldest treasurer, restored in the plain letters every ledger in history has used to count what he guards. Wealth needs no diacritics; it needs a vault, a guard, and a name — all three are here.

sources.name: Śiva and Skanda Purāṇas (the northern guardianship)

lore.archaeology: Kubera’s images ride the northern walls of every medieval Hindu temple as lokapāla; the Ajanta and Ellora caves give him early monumental form. In Nepal and Tibet his Jambhala bronzes are among the most produced ritual objects of the last millennium.
lore.cult: Merchants keep his pot; temples install him as vault-guardian; the Dipāvali season invokes him alongside Lakṣmī. His Buddhist cult is a regular monastery ritual — the Jambhala sādhana performed for the community’s material needs.
lore.iconography: Pot-bellied, bejewelled, with a money-bag and the mongoose; riding the mule-eyed man or the lion; in Buddhist form black or golden, holding the citron and the gem-spitting mongoose. His face is often asymmetric — the burned eye of the Paraśurāma legend.
lore.reception: Comparative religion lists him with Plutus and the Dagda as the fat treasurer-god type; Buddhist studies know him as the great example of a Hindu deity absorbed whole into the dharma. In modern India, ‘Kubera’ is simply the word for a very rich man.
